language_wrapper: On a circular board with {n} labeled vertices (0 through {n_minus_one}), vertex i initially holds the number of coins given in cyclic order by {coins}. In one operation, Kumar chooses an edge between two adjacent vertices whose endpoints both currently have at least one coin; he removes one coin from each of those two endpoints and keeps both coins for himself. No coins are added back to any vertex. He may perform operations in any order, and he stops when no edge has two endpoints with at least one coin each. Among all possible sequences of legal operations until stopping, let N_max be the maximum number of coins he can collect and N_min be the minimum number he must collect. Compute the value of 1000*N_max + N_min.
hardness_rationale: This family replaces the single-coin, three-vertex operation with a capacitated multi-step edge-removal process on a cycle. The extremal outcomes become (i) a maximum b-matching problem on a cycle (to maximize collected coins), and (ii) a minimum-over-maximal b-matching (equivalently, a maximum-weight independent set of residuals) to minimize collected coins. Both require advanced reasoning: mapping the dynamics to combinatorial optimization under capacity constraints, handling wrap-around, and ensuring maximality (no augmenting edge) via local saturation checks. Unlike the seed, which has uniform capacities and a single operation type, these instances demand graph-theoretic modeling and dynamic programming with global constraints, precluding trivial guesswork and necessitating rigorous invariants.
notes: Proof sketch: Model each operation as selecting an edge e_i = (i, i+1), decrementing the capacities at i and i+1 by 1 and collecting 2 coins. Let y_i be the number of times edge e_i is used. Then for each vertex i, the total consumption is y_{i-1} + y_i and must satisfy 0 <= y_{i-1} + y_i <= a_i. The final residual r_i = a_i - (y_{i-1} + y_i) is nonnegative. The process stops iff no edge has both endpoints with r > 0, i.e., the residual positives form an independent set: for all i, r_i * r_{i+1} = 0. The total number of operations is sum_i y_i, and the collected coins are 2*sum_i y_i. Therefore N_max equals 2 times the maximum b-matching size on the cycle with vertex capacities a_i. Our DP maximizes sum y_i subject to y_i >= 0 integer and y_{i-1} + y_i <= a_i, including wrap-around constraints by enumerating y_{n-1}. For N_min, among all maximal sequences (no augmenting edge), every edge must be incident to a saturated vertex (used exactly to capacity) on at least one endpoint: for each i, either y_{i-1} + y_i = a_i or y_i + y_{i+1} = a_{i+1}. Minimizing sum y_i under these constraints is equivalent to maximizing the residual sum sum r_i subject to independence, i.e., selecting a maximum-weight independent set where each selected vertex keeps all its coins. The provided DP enforces local maximality edge by edge while minimizing the total y. Both DPs are exact due to the cycle’s local constraints and the wrap-around enumeration. The verifier recomputes both extremes to ensure correctness and nontriviality.
source_question: Kumar has a regular 2024-gon, and there is a coin on each vertex of it. In one operation, he selects a vertex, takes one coin from each of the two adjacent vertices to this selected vertex, adds one coin to the selected vertex, and keeps the extra coin for himself. He can perform such an operation only when both of the two adjacent vertices have at least one coin. He stops when he can no longer perform any operation. Let the maximum value of the number of coins he can collect be \(N_{max}\), and the minimum value be \(N_{min}\). Find the value of \(1000\cdot N_{max}+N_{min}\).
